analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to pay Medicaid rebates so states pay no more than the manufacturer's best price anywhere.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a vote: introduced September 12, 1990 with 22 Democratic cosponsors, it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee's health subcommittee and died when the Congress ended January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made drug manufacturers pay quarterly rebates to state Medicaid programs so that states end up paying no more per prescription for brand-name drugs than the lowest price the manufacturer gives any other customer, and 10% back on other drugs. In exchange, states could not use formularies to block coverage of drugs from rebate-compliant makers, and states had to run 24-hour prior-approval systems and new prescription-safety review programs, with extra federal money to pay for them.
analysis.who_benefits: State Medicaid programs and their taxpayers, who would recover money from manufacturers on every prescription; Medicaid beneficiaries, who would keep guaranteed access to covered brand-name drugs even in states that use formularies; and physicians, whose prescribing choices would be protected by 24-hour, immediate-response prior-authorization systems.

how_it_helps.text: Drug makers would owe each state a quarterly rebate equal to the gap between their average wholesale price and their 'best price' — the lowest price they charge anyone in the country — plus a guaranteed 10% rebate on other covered drugs, so Medicaid would never pay more than the manufacturer's best customer.

States could not exclude, through formularies or similar restrictions, any drug from a rebate-compliant manufacturer when prescribed for a medically accepted use, and prior-approval programs would have to answer doctors immediately, 24 hours a day.

States would have to build drug-use review programs — checking prescriptions before and after they are filled for safety and appropriateness, plus physician and pharmacist education — with the federal government covering 75% of the cost.
Manufacturers that report false price information would face civil penalties up to $100,000 per item, and wholesalers and manufacturers refusing price verification could be fined up to $10,000.

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug manufacturers, who would pay quarterly rebates on Medicaid prescriptions, disclose their average and best prices to the government each quarter, and face daily fines and agreement suspension for late or false price reports.

drawbacks.text: The 'best price' formula would push manufacturers to avoid deep discounts anywhere in the market, since a bigger discount to any customer would raise the rebate owed on every Medicaid prescription — a mechanism that tends to flatten discounts rather than lower list prices.

By requiring states to cover all drugs from rebate-compliant makers for medically accepted uses, the bill would limit states' ability to steer patients to cheaper alternatives, and the enhanced 75% federal match for drug-review programs would add federal spending.
The bill takes on only Medicaid drug spending — roughly one slice of the drug market — rather than prices facing the broader public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it targets, the bill was a solid deal: states and taxpayers would recover money on prescriptions and beneficiaries would gain coverage guarantees, while the cost fell on manufacturers' margins. The main honest objection is design: the best-price formula rewards manufacturers for hiding discounts, and the coverage mandates plus the 75% federal match add real federal and state administrative cost. It was a targeted fix, not a broad drug-price solution.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which passed it along to its health subcommittee two weeks later, and no further action ever came — it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Wyden introduced the bill with Rep. Jim Cooper on September 12, 1990, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On September 28, 1990, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment — the last action ever recorded on it.
The bill attracted 22 cosponsors, all House Democrats, but never received a subcommittee markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers were better off: they avoided the quarterly rebates, mandatory best-price disclosure, and penalties the bill would have imposed, while state Medicaid programs kept paying prevailing market prices.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 22 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record — but the bill never reached a vote, so where the parties stood as a whole was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have taken a quarterly rebate on every Medicaid prescription — at least 10% and up to half the wholesale price — and forced disclosure of the lowest price they charge anyone, with fines for false reports. Their gain from the bill's death was the public's lost savings.

industries.industry: Generic and other non-innovator drug makers
industries.note: They would have owed a flat 10% rebate on the average manufacturer price of their drugs dispensed to Medicaid patients.

Wholesalers and pharmacies would face civil penalties up to $10,000 for refusing price-verification requests, but the bill's guaranteed coverage and 24-hour prior-approval rules would also smooth reimbursement for drugs they dispense to Medicaid patients.

The bill would have required quarterly reports on the identity and dosages of drugs they prescribe under Medicaid — an administrative burden, attached to a program that guaranteed their patients' drug coverage.
